title: Generative media platform
tagline: Turn a short brief into slides, narrated audio and infographics, with many model providers behind one gateway.
govtech_note:
Giant Robots Labs is GovTech's experimental lab in the Government Technology Office. Its pilots own a product end to end, including reliability and costs, and work with AI agents. Prism is one of its three featured products, listed as "a generative media platform for creating presentations, audio, diagrams, infographics, and other media".

Nothing else about Prism is public. Everything below is a reasonable design for a product like it, not how Prism is built.
summary:
Generation is slow (seconds to minutes) and costly per call, so every request becomes a job: POST /jobs returns 202 and a job id, and the client follows progress by polling or SSE. An orchestrator agent turns the brief into a structured JSON spec, which is the source of truth; worker pools on a queue make images and speech, and sandboxed renderers turn the spec into PPTX, PDF and PNG.

All model calls go through an LLM gateway that routes between providers, retries, falls back, enforces per-agency quotas, caches identical prompts and counts every token.

functional: Create a deck, infographic, diagram or narrated audio from a brief and a template
Show progress while a job runs (polling or SSE) and return download links
Regenerate or edit one slide without redoing the rest
Apply an agency's brand template (colours, fonts, logo, layouts) automatically
Human review and approval before an asset is shared
nonfunctional: Accept a job in under ~200 ms; a 12-slide deck ready in about 90 s
Survive one provider being down or rate-limited without failing jobs
Per-agency quotas and cost tracking down to the job
No PII or unsafe content in prompts sent out or in outputs shared
Generated files only reachable through short-lived signed URLs
out_of_scope: Training or fine-tuning our own models

estimates.label: Decks per day
estimates.calc: assume 20,000 active officers × 10% make one a day

Status, progress (slides done / total), errors per slide, artefact ids.
Server-Sent Events stream of progress; falls back to polling.

data.name: jobs

data.note: Mirrored nightly to Postgres for billing reports.

flows.name: Create a deck from a brief
flows.desc: The main path: brief in, spec out, slides rendered.

steps.note: Officer posts a brief, a template id and an Idempotency-Key. The API answers 202 Accepted with a job id in ~100 ms; the work itself takes 30-90 s, far too long to hold an HTTP request open.
Screen the brief before any model sees it: block disallowed content, and detect NRIC numbers, phone numbers and addresses so they are masked or the officer is warned.
Insert the job row with UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key), so a double-click or a retry returns the same job instead of paying for a second deck.
Hand the job to the orchestrator (via a queue in practice). The UI now opens an SSE stream on /jobs/{id}/events to show progress.
Ask the model for an outline as JSON matching a schema: slide ids, layouts from the template, titles, bullets, image prompts. Free text would be impossible to edit one slide at a time.
The gateway picks a provider and model for this task, checks the agency's token quota, and records tokens in and out against the job.
Validate the JSON against the schema (retry once with the error message if it fails), then save it as spec version 1. Every later step reads this spec, never the chat history.
Fan out one task per asset: 4 images, 12 slide previews. Each task key is (deck, slide, spec_version, kind), so a retried task overwrites instead of duplicating.
When the image tasks finish, a render task builds PPTX, PDF and PNG previews from the spec, the template's brand tokens and the stored images. The SSE stream sends done.

flows.name: Regenerate slide 3
flows.desc: Partial regeneration works because the spec, not the file, is the source of truth.

steps.note: Officer clicks "redo slide 3: shorter, add a chart". The API creates a small job that names the deck, slide_id and the spec version it was based on.
The orchestrator loads spec v4 and sends the model only slide 3, plus the deck title and the slides on either side as context. That is ~2k tokens instead of ~30k.
The new slide must match the same JSON schema. The gateway still meters it against the agency quota.
A redo deliberately skips the cache (the officer wants a different answer), but the cache still serves the unchanged prompts if the whole deck is rebuilt.
Write spec v5 with only slide 3 changed, using WHERE version = 4 so a concurrent manual edit is not overwritten. On conflict, ask the officer to retry.
Enqueue tasks only for what changed: one image, one preview. The other 11 slides keep their stored assets because their content hashes did not change.
An image worker takes the new image task.
The new PNG is stored under a content-hash key, so storing the same image twice is free.
Re-render the PPTX and PDF from spec v5 (~2 s; rendering is cheap, model calls are not). Old versions stay, so undo is just pointing at v4.

flows.name: Generate narrated audio
flows.desc: Text to speech for each slide, in parallel.

steps.note: Officer asks for narration in English for an approved deck. The API returns 202 and a job id.
The orchestrator asks the LLM to write a ~120-word script per slide from the spec, and stores it in the spec's narration field so the officer can edit the words before any audio is made.
Check the scripts as model output: PII the brief did not contain, unsafe content, or claims that need review. Flagged slides wait for a human.
One TTS task per slide. 12 slides of ~1 min each in parallel finish in about the time of the slowest one, not 12 minutes.
TTS workers pull tasks. The pool size is capped to stay under the TTS provider's concurrency limit, so a big job queues instead of getting 429s.
Speech also goes through the gateway: same quotas, retries and cost tracking (TTS is billed per character, not per token).
Each slide's MP3 (~1 MB per minute at 128 kbps) lands in storage; a final step joins them into one file and embeds them in the PPTX.
The officer's player fetches the audio through a signed URL valid for 15 minutes, so a leaked link stops working.
On a CDN miss the edge reads from the private bucket. The bucket itself is never public.

flows.name: Provider outage triggers fallback
flows.desc: The image provider starts failing during a busy morning.

steps.note: An image worker takes a task: "flat illustration, team meeting, brand palette".
The worker never calls a provider directly; it calls the gateway with a task type (image.illustration), not a vendor name.
Same model, params and prompt seen before? Return the stored image. Here it is a miss.
Primary returns 503 twice. The gateway retries with exponential backoff and jitter (200 ms, then 400 ms) but keeps the total under the task's 30 s budget.
Error rate over 50% for 30 s opens the circuit breaker for that provider. New calls skip it at once instead of each waiting through retries.
Route to the next provider on the approved list for this task type (one with acceptable data-handling terms). The response records which model actually produced the asset.
The worker gets the image and runs the output safety check. Fallback images may look different, so the slide is marked for the officer to glance at.
Store the image and finish the task. A probe request every 30 s closes the breaker once the primary recovers.

deep.title: The spec is the source of truth
deep.html:
The model never writes a PPTX. It writes a JSON spec: {template_id, slides: [{id, layout, title, bullets, image_prompt, asset_ids, narration}]}, validated against a schema. Renderers turn the spec plus the template into files.

  • Partial regeneration: "redo slide 3" replaces one object in slides; every other slide keeps its id and its assets.
  • Versions: specs are append-only (v1, v2, ...). Each render names the version it used, so undo and "what changed" are free.
  • Brand: colours, fonts, logo and layouts are design tokens on the template, not in the prompt. The model picks a layout name; it cannot pick a font. That keeps every agency's decks on brand, and changing a token re-renders old decks without a model call.
  • Manual edits are JSON patches to the same spec, so human and agent edits mix cleanly.

Infographics and diagrams use the same idea: the model outputs data (nodes, edges, numbers) and a deterministic renderer draws them, so labels are spelled right and numbers match.

deep.title: Worker pools on a queue
deep.html:
Each asset type has its own queue and pool, because they differ a lot: an LLM slide call takes ~5 s, an image ~10 s, a TTS minute ~3 s, a render ~2 s and uses CPU, not a provider.

  • A morning rush of 50 decks becomes ~200 image tasks. The queue absorbs the spike; the pool drains it at the rate the provider allows (14 concurrent calls in the estimates).
  • Workers ack a task only after the asset is stored. A crash means the task becomes visible again after its timeout and another worker redoes it. Tasks are idempotent because the output key is the task key.
  • After 3 failures a task goes to a dead-letter queue and the job shows that slide as failed with a retry button, instead of failing the whole deck.
  • Interactive jobs (an officer is watching) go on a higher-priority queue than bulk jobs (100 certificates overnight).

deep.title: The LLM gateway: routing, quotas and cost
deep.html:
Every model call (text, image, speech) goes through one gateway. It is the only service holding provider keys.

  • Routing: callers name a task type; a config table maps it to an ordered list of models. Swapping a model is a config change plus an eval run, not a deploy.
  • Rate limits and quotas: a token bucket per provider (stay under their limits) and per agency (monthly token budget). Over quota: queue bulk work, reject interactive work with a clear message.
  • Retries and fallbacks: retry 5xx and timeouts with backoff and jitter, never retry 4xx; circuit breaker per provider; fall back only to providers approved for that data classification.
  • Cache: key = SHA-256 of (model, params, template version, prompt). Exact match only; a semantic cache could return a slide about the wrong ministry.
  • Cost: log tokens, characters and images per call with job, agency and task type. Dashboards show spend per agency per day and alert when a job passes its budget, which is how you catch an agent stuck in a loop.

deep.title: Safety, human review and evals
deep.html:
Inputs: block disallowed requests and detect PII (NRIC, phone, email, address) in the brief and uploads before they leave for a third-party model. Outputs: run the same checks on generated text, plus an image safety classifier, because a model can invent a realistic-looking NRIC.

Human review: nothing is shared outside the creator's workspace until a person approves it. Flagged slides show the reason.

Evals: keep a regression set of ~200 briefs. On every prompt, template or model change, generate decks and grade a sample against a rubric (follows the brief, factual to the source, on-brand layout, no PII, readable) using an LLM grader that is spot-checked by humans each week. A drop of more than a few points blocks the change. Sample ~1% of production jobs into the same grading for drift.

tradeoffs.choice: Answer in the request or run a job?
tradeoffs.pick: Job: 202 + job id, SSE or polling
tradeoffs.why: A deck takes 30-90 s and fans out to dozens of calls. Holding a request open hits load-balancer timeouts and loses all work when the connection drops; a job survives and can be retried.

tradeoffs.choice: Let the model write files, or a structured spec?
tradeoffs.why: A spec can be validated, versioned, diffed and partly regenerated, and brand rules are applied by code. A model-written PPTX can only be regenerated whole.

tradeoffs.choice: Call one provider directly, or a gateway?
tradeoffs.why: One place for keys, quotas, retries, fallback and cost data. Costs one extra hop (~5 ms), which is nothing next to a 5 s model call.
Renderers parse model output and user uploads, both untrusted. Run them in containers with no network, read-only filesystem, CPU and memory limits and a 60 s timeout.
Exact hits are always correct. A semantic cache saves more but can return a near match about the wrong agency or date, which is worse than paying for a call.

bottlenecks.issue: Provider rate limits at the morning peak (429s)
bottlenecks.fix: Cap each worker pool below the provider limit, let the queue hold the backlog, put interactive jobs ahead of bulk ones, and spread load over a second provider.

bottlenecks.issue: An agent loop or a 200-slide brief burns tokens
bottlenecks.fix: Per-job token budget and max planning steps, checked in the gateway; stop the job and tell the officer instead of spending more.

bottlenecks.issue: A render hangs on a huge table or a malformed image
bottlenecks.fix: Hard timeout and memory limit per render; mark that slide failed and render the rest.

bottlenecks.issue: Spec store gets hot from progress updates
bottlenecks.fix: Keep live progress in Redis and push it over SSE; write to Postgres only on state changes.

followups.q: How do you make "redo slide 3" cheap and safe?
followups.a: Keep the spec as the source of truth. Send the model only slide 3 plus nearby context, write a new spec version with a version check, and re-render. Unchanged slides keep their assets because their content hashes match.

followups.q: A provider changes its model and quality drops. How would you notice?
followups.a: Pin model versions in the gateway config. Run the regression set and rubric grading before any switch, and grade ~1% of production jobs daily so drift shows up as a falling score per task type.

followups.q: How do you stop one agency using up everyone's capacity?
followups.a: A token bucket per agency in the gateway for both rate and monthly budget, plus fair scheduling in the queue (round-robin across agencies) so one bulk job cannot starve other users.

followups.q: Can a brief with NRIC numbers reach a third-party model?
followups.a: Not by default: the input check detects NRIC patterns (letter, 7 digits, checksum letter) and masks or blocks them. Routing also respects data classification, so sensitive jobs go only to approved models.

followups.q: Why SSE and not WebSockets for progress?
followups.a: Progress flows one way, server to browser. SSE is plain HTTP, reconnects on its own with Last-Event-ID, and passes through proxies easily. Polling every 2 s is the fallback.

quiz.q: Why does POST /jobs return 202 instead of the finished deck?
options: Generation takes up to minutes, so the work runs as a job the client can follow and retry
Browsers cannot download PPTX from a POST
quiz.why: Long work behind a short request hits timeouts and is lost on disconnect. A job id lets the client poll or stream progress.

quiz.q: What makes regenerating one slide possible without touching the others?
options: Keeping a versioned JSON spec with stable slide ids as the source of truth
quiz.why: The renderer rebuilds files from the spec, so changing one slide object changes one slide.

quiz.q: The primary image provider returns 503 on half its calls. What should the gateway do?
options: Open a circuit breaker and route to an approved fallback provider
Fail all jobs until it recovers
quiz.why: Bounded retries with backoff, then a breaker stops wasting time on a sick provider while a fallback keeps jobs moving.

quiz.q: Which cache key is safe for identical prompts?
options: A hash of model, parameters, template version and prompt
quiz.why: The same prompt to a different model or template should give a different result, so all of them belong in the key.

quiz.q: Why put TTS and image generation on separate queues?
options: They have different speeds and provider limits, so each pool is sized and capped on its own
Queues cannot hold mixed message types
quiz.why: One shared pool lets slow image calls block quick TTS calls and makes per-provider concurrency caps impossible.
